summary: Verified Taiwanese evidence links traffic-related and general ambient air pollution with child asthma (CO/NOx, Guo 1999; Hwang 2005), lower lung function in 6-24 year olds (PM2.5, about -2 to -3% per 10 ug/m3, Guo 2019; PM10 in schoolchildren, Tsui 2018), ADHD diagnosis after prenatal and early-life PM2.5 (HR 1.26 per 10 ug/m3 in first trimester), vascular dementia (NO2 >75th percentile vs <25th, OR about 2), cognitive impairment and stroke in older adults, and higher oxidative-stress and exhaled-CO markers in people working beside traffic (toll workers, delivery workers). Every study used station-based, modelled or traffic-density exposure. None isolates scooters, none measures pedestrians at a red light or in a two-stage turn box, and most are cross-sectional or case-control, so they show association, not proof of cause. Results that cut against over-claiming must be stated: PM10 was inversely related to asthma in Hwang 2005; asthma symptoms fell while diagnoses rose 1995-2001; the non-smoker delivery-worker CO gap is only 0.44 ppm; the scooter studies (Chan 1993, Lee 2005) concern the older two-stroke fleet. WHO/UNICEF/RCP child-vulnerability text, official 65+ share, MOTC mode shares, Taiwan Children Health Study and Changhua CARE remain unverified (search budget exhausted in this check).

findings.claim: In a nationwide Taiwanese survey of middle-school students, asthma prevalence was associated with traffic-related air pollution, especially CO and nitrogen oxides, after adjusting for age, eczema history and parental education.
findings.value: 331,686 non-smoking children in schools within 2 km of 55 monitoring stations; no single effect size in abstract
findings.setting: Taiwan nationwide, middle-school children, 1995-96 survey, station data
findings.exposureType: traffic markers (CO, NOx) from ambient stations
findings.citation: Guo YL, Lin YC, Sung FC, Huang SL, Ko YC, Lai JS, Su HJ, Shaw CK, Lin RS, Dockery DW. 1999. Climate, traffic-related air pollutants, and asthma prevalence in middle-school children in Taiwan. Environ Health Perspect 107(12):1001-1006.
findings.quote: Asthma prevalence rates adjusted for age, history of atopic eczema, and parental education were associated with nonsummer (June-August) temperature, winter (January-March) humidity, and traffic-related air pollution, especially carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides
findings.caveats: Ecological exposure (station within 2 km of school), not personal; cross-sectional; CO/NOx reflect all traffic, not scooters; 1995-96 fleet and fuel differ from today's.
findings.useOnSite: A large Taiwanese national survey found children at schools with higher traffic-related pollution (CO, NOx) had more asthma; it cannot separate scooters from other traffic.
findings.verifierNote: Abstract opened via Europe PMC and Crossref (vol 107, issue 12, pp 1001-1006). All claims match.

findings.claim: In 32,672 Taiwanese school children, asthma risk was positively associated with CO and ozone, NOx was not clearly associated, and PM10 was weakly inversely associated, so the evidence is mixed by pollutant.
findings.setting: Taiwan nationwide, school children, 2001 questionnaire (93% response), mean of 2000 monthly station averages
findings.citation: Hwang BF, Lee YL, Lin YC, Jaakkola JJ, Guo YL. 2005. Traffic related air pollution as a determinant of asthma among Taiwanese school children. Thorax 60(6):467-473.
findings.quote: the risk of childhood asthma was positively associated with O3 (adjusted OR 1.138, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.001 to 1.293), CO (adjusted OR 1.045, 95% CI 1.017 to 1.074), and NOx (adjusted OR 1.005, 95% CI 0.954 to 1.117)
findings.caveats: CO effect small per 100 ppb; NOx interval includes 1; PM10 and SO2 went the opposite way ('Against our prior hypothesis'); ozone is secondary. Do not claim all pollutants raise asthma.
findings.useOnSite: Taiwanese school-child data link long-term CO (a traffic marker) to higher asthma odds, but the picture across pollutants is mixed and the effect per unit is small.
findings.verifierNote: All numbers match the abstract. The stray 'scooter' field in the original was dropped. Abstract's own conclusion: consistent with long-term traffic-related NOx, CO, O3 raising asthma risk, although the NOx estimate itself is null.

findings.claim: Flexural eczema in Taiwanese middle-school children was associated with traffic-related pollutants (NOx, CO); recurrent eczema only in girls.
findings.value: 317,926 children within 2 km of 55 stations; recurrent eczema 2.4% (boys) / 2.3% (girls); flexural eczema 1.7% both sexes
findings.citation: Lee YL, Su HJ, Sheu HM, Yu HS, Guo YL. 2008. Traffic-related air pollution, climate, and prevalence of eczema in Taiwanese school children. J Invest Dermatol 128(10):2412-2420.
findings.quote: flexural eczema was found to be associated with traffic-related air pollutants, including nitrogen oxides and carbon monoxide
findings.caveats: Skin outcome, not respiratory; ecological; no effect sizes in abstract; mid-1990s data.
findings.useOnSite: Optional supporting point only; not central to the pavement-breathing scene.

findings.claim: Among 24,544 Taiwanese people aged 6-24, a 10 ug/m3 higher 2-year average PM2.5 was associated with about 2-3% lower lung function and 20% higher odds of poor lung function.
findings.setting: Taiwan, 6-24-year-olds, 33,506 observations 2000-2014, spatiotemporal PM2.5 model at home address
findings.citation: Guo C, Hoek G, Chang LY, Bo Y, Lin C, Huang B, Chan TC, Tam T, Lau AKH, Lao XQ. 2019. Long-Term Exposure to Ambient Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) and Lung Function in Children, Adolescents, and Young Adults: A Longitudinal Cohort Study. Environ Health Perspect 127(12):127008.
findings.quote: Every 10-μg/m3 increase in the 2-y average PM2.5 concentration was associated with decreases of 2.22% [95% confidence interval (CI): -2.60, -1.85], 2.94 (95% CI: -3.36, -2.51), and 2.79% (95% CI: -3.15, -2.41) in the FVC, FEV1, and MMEF, respectively.
findings.caveats: General regional PM2.5, not traffic-specific or roadside; participants are health-screening attendees up to age 24; residual confounding possible.
findings.useOnSite: Long-term exposure to ambient PM2.5 in Taiwan was linked to smaller lung capacity in people aged 6-24; the study measured regional air, not street corners.
findings.verifierNote: Numbers match the abstract exactly. The abstract's 'poor lung function' is described as a 20% increase in prevalence (OR 1.20).

findings.claim: In 1,016 non-asthmatic Taiwanese schoolchildren, lifetime residential PM10 exposure was associated with lower lung function, independent of other pollutants.
findings.setting: 44 schools in Taiwan, children aged 6-15, 2011 survey; kriged EPA station data
findings.citation: Tsui HC, Chen CH, Wu YH, Chiang HC, Chen BY, Guo YL. 2018. Lifetime exposure to particulate air pollutants is negatively associated with lung function in non-asthmatic children. Environ Pollut 236:953-961.
findings.quote: a 10 μg/m3 increase in PM10 was related to reductions in the forced expiratory volume in 1 s (-2.00%; 95% confidence interval [CI] -3.09% to -0.90%)
findings.caveats: General ambient PM10, not traffic-specific; cross-sectional; station-based kriging means misclassification likely.
findings.useOnSite: Taiwanese children with higher lifetime PM10 exposure had measurably lower lung function, though the pollution is general ambient air.
findings.verifierNote: Numbers match. Results are after adjustment for 7-day average pollutant levels.

findings.claim: In 4,736 school children near industrial/coal-power areas of central Taiwan, annual PM2.5 was associated with higher odds of physician-diagnosed asthma and with higher exhaled nitric oxide (airway inflammation).
findings.value: Physician-diagnosed asthma OR 1.595; exercise-induced wheeze OR 1.726 (increment not stated in abstract); +1 ug/m3 annual PM2.5 = +1.0% FENO
findings.setting: Six townships near industrial areas / coal-based power plants, central Taiwan, land-use-regression PM2.5
findings.citation: Tsai YG, Chio CP, Yang KD, Lin CH, Yeh YP, Chang YJ, Chien JW, Wang SL, Huang SK, Chan CC. 2025 (online Jan 2024). Long-term PM2.5 exposure is associated with asthma prevalence and exhaled nitric oxide levels in children. Pediatr Res 97(1):370-377.
findings.quote: An increase of 1 μg/m3 annual PM2.5 exposure was significantly associated with a 1.0% increase in FENO levels
findings.caveats: Industrial/coal-plant setting, not a traffic or scooter study; OR increment not stated in abstract, so do not quote ORs without the full paper; cross-sectional. The abstract also lists living 'near the road' among correlates of higher FENO, a traffic-relevant but unquantified hint.
findings.useOnSite: Use only as general evidence that PM2.5 is linked to child airway inflammation in Taiwan; do not attribute it to scooters.
findings.verifierNote: Abstract matches. Crossref: Pediatric Research 97(1):370-377, issued online 2024-01-23. Added the 'near the road' observation.

findings.claim: Taiwanese ISAAC surveys of 12-15-year-olds show lifetime physician-diagnosed asthma rose between 1995-96 and 2001 (more in girls) while 12-month asthma symptoms fell (boys) or stabilized (girls), so a simple 'asthma is rising because of scooters' claim is not supported.
findings.value: 44,104 participants in 1995-96; 11,048 in 2001; no percentages in abstract
findings.citation: Lee YL, Hwang BF, Lin YC, Guo YL; Taiwan Childhood Allergy Survey Group. 2007. Time trend of asthma prevalence among school children in Taiwan. Pediatr Allergy Immunol 18(3):188-195.
findings.quote: Over the past decade in Taiwan, the lifetime prevalence of childhood asthma was increasing, more marked among girls; however, the 12-month prevalence of asthma symptoms was decreasing, mostly among boys.
findings.caveats: Data end in 2001; trend is not linked to traffic; authors suggest better awareness and management might explain falling symptoms. No post-2010 official prevalence verified.
findings.useOnSite: Cite only for the historic trend and say recent official prevalence was not verified.
findings.verifierNote: Matches abstract. The 'not supported' conclusion is the checker's inference about site claims, not the authors'.

findings.claim: In a Taiwanese birth cohort of 425,736 term singleton children, higher PM2.5 in the first trimester and in early life (years 1-3) was associated with higher risk of ADHD diagnosis.
findings.value: First-trimester HR 1.26 (95% CI 1.13-1.40) per 10 ug/m3 PM2.5, rising at PM2.5 above 16 ug/m3; postnatal HR 1.40-1.87 at years 1-3 (increment not stated in abstract); 9,294 ADHD cases
findings.setting: Taiwan, singleton live term births 2004-2015, 1-km satellite PM2.5
findings.citation: Chang YC, Chen WT, Su SH, Jung CR, Hwang BF. 2022. PM2.5 exposure and incident attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder during the prenatal and postnatal periods: A birth cohort study. Environ Res 214:113769.
findings.quote: The hazard ratio (HR) of ADHD was significantly associated with a 10 μg/m3 increase in PM2.5 during the first trimester (HR = 1.26; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.13-1.40)
findings.caveats: General ambient PM2.5; observational; ADHD diagnosis (registry), not birth weight. Cohort is of term births, so preterm infants are excluded. The 1.40-1.87 postnatal range has no stated increment in the abstract, so do not present it as 'per 10 ug/m3'. Abstract reports the risk rising above 16 ug/m3 and sharply above 50 ug/m3 in year 3; the 'sex modification' was not significant.
findings.useOnSite: A large Taiwanese birth cohort links higher PM2.5 in pregnancy and early life with higher ADHD diagnosis rates; an association with general air pollution.
findings.verifierNote: Core numbers confirmed. Corrected: postnatal HR increment unspecified; added threshold information and the term-births restriction. Authors write 'may increase the risk', so keep causal wording hedged.

findings.claim: In a Taiwanese cohort of pregnant women, PM2.5, NO2, SO2 and CO in the 30 days before delivery were inversely associated with birth length.
findings.value: No effect sizes or sample size in abstract
findings.setting: Taiwan, women recruited in second trimester, gestational hypertension vs normotensive; ambient monitoring-station exposure
findings.citation: Hung TH, Hsu TY, Ou CY, Lo LM, Shaw SW, Wan GH. 2026. Late-pregnancy air pollution exposure and neonatal anthropometry with and without gestational hypertension. iScience 29(8):117029.
findings.quote: PM2.5, NO2, SO2, and CO exposures were inversely associated with birth length.
findings.caveats: Abstract does not say 'hospital' cohort or give sample size; general ambient pollutants; birth length, not birth weight (lower birth weight in the abstract is tied to gestational hypertension, not to pollution); mediation by measured inflammatory markers was null.
findings.useOnSite: Preliminary Taiwanese data hint at shorter newborn length with higher late-pregnancy pollution; limited and not traffic-specific.
findings.verifierNote: Quote confirmed. Corrected: removed 'hospital' (not in abstract), added issue number from Crossref (29(8)), clarified that the birth-weight finding relates to hypertension.

findings.claim: In Taiwanese adults over 65, higher past NO2 exposure was associated with about double the odds of vascular dementia.
findings.value: NO2 >75th vs <25th percentile: OR 2.22 (95% CI 1.35-3.65) within 5 years and 2.05 (1.28-3.28) within 7 years before diagnosis; 25th-50th OR 1.62 and 50th-75th OR 1.61 at 5 years; 831 cases, 3,324 controls
findings.setting: Taiwan, National Health Insurance 1-million cohort, diagnoses 2005-2013, kriged data from 76 stations
findings.exposureType: NO2 (largely vehicle-derived in cities, per authors; also industry/power), modelled from stations
findings.citation: Li CY, Li CH, Martini S, Hou WH. 2019. Association between air pollution and risk of vascular dementia: A multipollutant analysis in Taiwan. Environ Int 133:105233.
findings.quote: Compared with the <25th percentile of NO2 exposure, the 25th-50th, 50th-75th, and >75th percentiles of NO2 exposure significantly increased ORs (95% confidence intervals): 1.62 (1.28-2.23), 1.61 (1.11-2.33), and 2.22 (1.35-3.65) within 5 years before diagnosis
findings.caveats: Fixed-station kriged exposure, not personal; case-control cannot prove cause; the authors say future studies should identify specific NO2 sources; coarse PM and CO were only 'sporadically' associated; the dose-response is not monotonic (OR 1.62 and 1.61 for the middle quartiles).
findings.useOnSite: Older Taiwanese adults with higher long-term NO2, which in cities mostly comes from vehicle exhaust, had higher odds of vascular dementia; scooters were not isolated.
findings.verifierNote: Corrected: the reference category is the <25th percentile (original text was garbled); added intermediate ORs and caveats. The authors' statement that most urban NO2 comes from motor-vehicle exhaust is general, not measured in this study.

findings.claim: A nationwide Taiwanese case-control study found short-, medium- and long-term PM2.5 exposure associated with incident ischemic stroke.
findings.value: 10,035 ischemic stroke cases, each matched to 2 controls; effect sizes not in abstract
findings.citation: Yang CP, Li CY, Huang WJ, Yu HL, Yang CC, Lu MC, Lang HC, Yan YH. 2021. Short-, Mid-, and Long-Term Associations Between PM2.5 and Stroke Incidence in Taiwan. J Occup Environ Med 63(9):742-751.
findings.quote: There were significant short-term, medium-term, and long-term relationships between PM2.5 exposure and ischemic stroke incidence.
findings.caveats: No numbers in the abstract; general ambient PM2.5; age-group results not seen; the abstract's own conclusion is that PM2.5 'should be considered a risk factor'.
findings.useOnSite: Taiwanese national data support PM2.5 as a risk factor for ischemic stroke; the study is about general air, not scooters.
findings.verifierNote: Matches abstract; Crossref gives vol 63, issue 9.

findings.claim: In Kaohsiung, on warm days, daily stroke admissions rose with PM10 and NO2; after two-pollutant adjustment only PM10 and NO2 stayed significant.
findings.value: 23,179 stroke admissions 1997-2000; per interquartile-range increase in PM10 / NO2: primary intracerebral hemorrhage RR 1.54 (1.31-1.81) / 1.56 (1.32-1.84); ischemic stroke RR 1.46 (1.32-1.61) / 1.55 (1.40-1.71)
findings.setting: Kaohsiung, Taiwan, time-stratified case-crossover, general ambient pollution
findings.exposureType: general ambient (PM10, NO2, CO, SO2, O3)
findings.citation: Tsai SS, Goggins WB, Chiu HF, Yang CY. 2003. Evidence for an association between air pollution and daily stroke admissions in Kaohsiung, Taiwan. Stroke 34(11):2612-2616.
findings.quote: We observed estimated relative risks of 1.54 (95% confidence interval [95%], 1.31 to 1.81) and 1.56 (95% CI, 1.32 to 1.84) for primary intracerebral hemorrhage for each interquartile range increase in PM10 and NO2.
findings.caveats: Dated; warm days (>=20 C) only for most associations (on cool days only CO and ischemic stroke); CO, SO2, O3 effects were mostly nonsignificant once NO2 or PM10 was controlled; the study does not isolate scooters.
findings.useOnSite: Older Taiwanese time-series evidence ties short-term PM10 and NO2 increases to stroke admissions on warm days.
findings.verifierNote: Corrected: original claim implied five pollutants all robust and omitted numbers; abstract shows only PM10 and NO2 survive two-pollutant models. Added RRs and the cool-day result.

findings.claim: In 35,195 Taiwan Biobank participants aged over 60, higher PM2.5 and SO2 exposure tertiles were associated with higher odds of mild cognitive impairment.
findings.value: PM2.5 OR 1.23 (95% CI 1.11-1.37); SO2 OR 1.20 (1.07-1.34); highest tertile of both OR 2.33 (1.56-3.48); 4,173 MCI cases vs 31,022 controls (11.9%); mean PM2.5 30.7 ug/m3
findings.setting: Taiwan Biobank, age >60, 2008-2021, nearest EPA station
findings.citation: Su SL, Lin YT, Pan CH, Lee MC, Chen YH, Lin HT, Su H, Chen WT. 2026. The association between air pollutants and mild cognitive impairment in Taiwanese elderly. Int J Med Sci 23(6):2072-2080.
findings.quote: higher exposure to PM2.5 and SO2 are associated with a higher risk of MCI compared to that of lower exposure levels (OR = 1.23, 95% CI: 1.11-1.37; OR = 1.20, 95% CI: 1.07-1.34)
findings.caveats: Cross-sectional; nearest-station exposure; the abstract does not state NO2/CO results; SO2 points to non-traffic sources (checker's inference); 'synergistic interaction' is the authors' wording, and the combined OR is still observational.
findings.useOnSite: Recent Taiwanese biobank data link PM2.5 to cognitive impairment in older adults; they do not isolate traffic.
findings.verifierNote: Numbers match the abstract. Comparison group is described only as 'lower exposure' tertiles; 'top vs bottom' is a reasonable but unstated reading.

findings.claim: Female highway toll-station workers exposed to traffic exhaust had about double the urinary 8-OHdG of office workers, and 8-OHdG rose with urinary 1-OHPG.
findings.value: Non-smokers: 13.6 vs 7.3 ug/g creatinine (difference 6.3, 95% CI 3.0-9.6); log(8-OHdG) vs log(1-OHPG) beta 0.372 (0.081-0.663); 47 exposed, 27 reference
findings.setting: Taiwan, female highway toll-station workers; exposure by traffic density and urinary 1-OHPG
findings.exposureType: traffic exhaust (mixed highway traffic), biomarker plus traffic density
findings.citation: Lai CH, Liou SH, Lin HC, Shih TS, Tsai PJ, Chen JS, Yang T, Jaakkola JJ, Strickland PT. 2005. Exposure to traffic exhausts and oxidative DNA damage. Occup Environ Med 62(4):216-222.
findings.quote: The mean concentration of urinary 8-OHdG was substantially higher among the exposed non-smokers (13.6 microg/g creatinine) compared with the reference non-smokers (7.3 microg/g creatinine; difference 6.3, 95% CI 3.0 to 9.6).
findings.caveats: Small, women only; highway traffic mostly cars and trucks; biomarker of oxidative stress, not disease; cross-sectional; plasma NO difference was not significant (CI -0.4 to 21.2).
findings.useOnSite: A Taiwanese study of people who stand beside heavy traffic all day found higher urinary markers of oxidative DNA damage; it shows a biological effect, not disease.

findings.claim: Taiwanese food-delivery workers had higher exhaled CO than a reference group, including among non-smokers.
findings.value: All: 4.79 vs 1.51 ppm (p<0.001); non-smokers: 1.57 vs 1.13 ppm (p=0.002); workers who smoke 14.46 ppm; 156 workers vs 49 reference; 25.0% of workers vs 4.1% of reference smoked
findings.setting: Taiwan, online food-delivery workers; exhaled-breath CO; vehicle type not stated in abstract
findings.exposureType: traffic exhaust inferred from exhaled CO; not scooter-confirmed
findings.citation: Li KH, Cheng YY, Huang SC, Chen CA, Lu JY, Chao ZT, Tseng YC, Guo HR. 2025. Assessing Carbon Monoxide Exposure in Food Delivery Workers by Using Exhaled Air with Consideration of Smoking Habits. J Epidemiol Glob Health 15(1):124.
findings.quote: amongst non-smokers, the CO concentration was still higher in food delivery workers than in the reference group (1.57 ppm vs. 1.13 ppm, p = 0.002)
findings.caveats: Non-smoker gap is 0.44 ppm; smoking dominates the all-worker figure ('smoking might contribute 89% of the CO' among smokers); small reference group; CO is an exposure marker, not a health outcome; the abstract does not say workers rode scooters.
findings.useOnSite: Delivery workers breathe out more CO than comparison people, but among non-smokers the difference is small, so say 'higher exposure', not 'poisoned'.
findings.verifierNote: Numbers confirmed. Corrected: original 'mostly motorcycle riders' is not in the abstract; scooterSpecific changed to 'not stated'; added smoker proportions.

findings.claim: In winter 1992 Taipei, students commuting by motorcycle were exposed to higher VOC concentrations than on buses, and Taipei commuters had about 3-8 times the VOC levels of Los Angeles commuters.
findings.value: Mean benzene in buses 173 ug/m3 (motorcycle value missing from the abstract text); road VOCs about 5x classroom VOCs; commute 45 min (elementary) to 95 min (vocational)
findings.setting: Taipei City, winter 1992, three commuting routes, 19 VOCs on Tenax tubes
findings.citation: Chan CC, Lin SH, Her GR. 1993. Student's exposure to volatile organic compounds while commuting by motorcycle and bus in Taipei City. J Air Waste Manage Assoc 43(9):1231-1238.
findings.quote: Higher VOC concentrations were measured on motorcycles than in buses.
findings.caveats: Over 30 years old (older fleet and fuels); abstract truncated at 250 words; measures riders and bus passengers, not pedestrians; VOC concentrations did not differ significantly by time of day or route.
findings.useOnSite: Historic Taipei measurements found motorcycle commuters breathed more VOCs than bus commuters; do not present the numbers as today's levels.
findings.verifierNote: Abstract matches; Crossref lists the journal as 'Air & Waste' (the predecessor of JAWMA), vol 43(9).

findings.claim: Particles from two-stroke motorcycle engines triggered IL-8 inflammatory signalling and oxidative stress in human airway cells in the laboratory.
findings.setting: In vitro, A549 human airway epithelial cells; filter-trapped particles from unleaded-gasoline two-stroke motorcycle engines
findings.citation: Lee CC, Cheng YW, Kang JJ. 2005. Motorcycle exhaust particles induce IL-8 production through NF-kappaB activation in human airway epithelial cells. J Toxicol Environ Health A 68(17-18):1537-1555.
findings.quote: filter-trapped particles emitted from unleaded gasoline-fueled, two-stroke motorcycle engines induce an increase in IL-8 production by activation of NF-kappaB in human airway epithelial cells
findings.caveats: Cell study; two-stroke engines are largely phased out (the phase-out claim is not in the paper); doses are not comparable with pavement exposure.
findings.useOnSite: Mechanistic support only: older two-stroke scooter exhaust particles inflamed human airway cells in the lab.
findings.verifierNote: Abstract matches. It also notes a previous mouse study with the same particles.

doNotClaim: That any Taiwanese study measured pedestrians at a red light next to idling scooters or in a two-stage turn box; none was found.
That the bad smell is itself a measure of dose or harm: odour reflects compounds detectable at very low levels and does not map to PM2.5 or toxic dose.

That scooters (rather than all traffic) caused the asthma, lung-function, stroke or dementia associations: all use station-based or modelled ambient exposure with markers shared by cars, trucks and buses.
That the 2019 EHP lung-function paper (Guo C et al.) is a traffic or scooter study; it is regional PM2.5.

That child asthma in Taiwan is rising because of traffic: the 1995-2001 trend showed rising lifetime diagnosis but falling 12-month symptoms, and Hwang 2005 found PM10 inversely associated with asthma.
That children breathe 'closer to the tailpipe' with a quoted number: WHO/UNICEF/RCP wording was not verified.
That the old two-stroke findings (Lee 2005 in vitro, Chan 1993 VOCs) describe today's fleet.
That delivery workers are 'poisoned by CO': the non-smoker gap is 0.44 ppm and the abstract does not state they rode scooters.
That the combined PM2.5+SO2 OR of 2.33 or the vascular-dementia ORs prove cause, or that SO2 and PM2.5 effects are traffic effects.
That the ADHD postnatal HR range 1.40-1.87 is per 10 ug/m3 (increment not given in the abstract).
That all pollutants raise child asthma (PM10 and SO2 were inversely or not associated in Hwang 2005).
Any official figure for Taiwan's 65+ share, child asthma prevalence or MOTC mode share: none verified.
gaps: WHO 2018 'Air pollution and child health', UNICEF 'Clear the air for children' / 'Danger in the air', Royal College of Physicians 'Every breath we take': not verified (search budget exhausted during this check).
Official statistics not verified: Ministry of the Interior 65+ share and super-aged date; MOHW/HPA child asthma prevalence; MOTC mode-share by age and income (environmental-justice item).
Taiwan Children Health Study and Changhua CARE papers: not found or checked; no effect sizes.
School-gate / drop-off exposure and school-commute exposure in Taiwan: nothing found.
Traffic-specific Taiwanese pregnancy evidence (low birth weight, preterm birth): not found; only general PM2.5 results.
Traffic police, street vendors, parking attendants with 1-OHP / 8-OHdG: only Lai 2005 toll workers; recent PM2.5/black carbon on scooter commutes in Taiwan not found.
Arcade (騎樓) business and ground-floor home exposure studies: none found.
Hanoi / Ho Chi Minh City / Bangkok scooter evidence: not checked in this pass.
Near-road concentration gradients and queue-start spikes at Taiwanese junctions (core of the red-light scene): not found.
Exact verification of full texts: only abstracts (Europe PMC) and Crossref metadata were opened; increments and subgroup results not in abstracts remain unchecked.
